extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of journalism, political science, and public policy; general readers interested in the press and public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical and practical criteria for how newspapers and experts create, present, and influence public opinion — including selection, sourcing, the difference between news and truth, the role of institutions, and the role of experts/social science in making facts reportable and usable for decision-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Every newspaper when it reaches the reader is the result of a whole series of selections as to what items shall be printed, in what position they shall be printed, how much space each shall occupy, what emphasis each shall have. There are no objective standards here. There are conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors exercise judgment about what will absorb a certain set of readers' attention; choices of headline, placement, space and emphasis shape what readers notice and how they interpret events (example: contrasting headlines about foreign policy vs a gossipy human-interest item).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stereotypes as cues for reader identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader must find a familiar foothold in the story, and this is supplied to him by the use of stereotypes. They tell him that if an association of plumbers is called a 'combine' it is appropriate to develop his hostility; if it is called a 'group of leading business men' the cue is for a favorable reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stereotypes simplify complex events and invite personal identification, but they also bias readers' reactions; awareness of this mechanism is essential for evaluating how news frames issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Securing attention by provoking feeling and personal identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem of securing attention is by no means equivalent to displaying the news in the perspective laid down by religious teaching or by some form of ethical culture. It is a problem of provoking feeling in the reader, of inducing him to feel a sense of personal identification with the stories he is reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News that fails to offer an opportunity for the reader to identify with the struggle depicted will not appeal widely; this commercial/psychological imperative shapes editorial decisions and can produce partisanship that is hard to reverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorials as reinforcers and clarifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials reinforce. Sometimes in a situation that on the news pages is too confusing to permit of identification, they give the reader a clue by means of which he engages himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorials can supply the 'suggestion' readers need to integrate feelings with the news, especially when the news is complex; this makes editorials powerful agents in shaping opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between news and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis... is that news and truth are not the same thing, and must be clearly distinguished. The function of news is to signalize an event, the function of truth is to bring to light the hidden facts, to set them into relation with each other, and make a picture of reality on which men can act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only where social conditions take measurable shape do news and truth coincide; treating news as equivalent to truth is a misleading standard of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of news depends on precision of event recording
rubrics_metrics.description: The news, as we have seen, is precise in proportion to the precision with which the event is recorded. Unless the event is capable of being named, measured, given shape, made specific, it either fails to take on the character of news, or it is subject to the accidents and prejudices of observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact tests of news exist only in limited domains (e.g., public records); beyond those domains reportage is more liable to observation bias and interpretive variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility in judging source reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper can be asked to take the responsibility of not making Lenin more dead than the source of the news is reliable; if there is one subject on which editors are most responsible it is in their judgment of the reliability of the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assert a fact as news when it rests on unreliable sources; the proper formulation is to report the claim and the source (example: report 'Helsingfors says Lenin is dead' rather than 'Lenin dead').

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic humility about unverifiable truth
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no discipline in applied psychology, as there is a discipline in medicine, engineering, or even law, which has authority to direct the journalist's mind when he passes from the news to the vague realm of truth... his own opinion is in some vital measure constructed out of his own stereotypes, according to his own code, and by the urgency of his own interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should recognize subjective lenses and temper assurance; where no objective test exists, journalists' versions of truth are provisional and constructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press is no substitute for institutional knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The press is no substitute for institutions. It is like the beam of a searchlight that moves restlessly about, bringing one episode and then another out of darkness into vision. Men cannot do the work of the world by this light alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expecting the press to furnish the continuous, comprehensive knowledge required for democratic decision-making is unrealistic; quality of news is an index of social organization and availability of institutional records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposing unrealistic expectations on the press (omnicompetent citizen model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory that the press can itself record those forces is false... the single reader as theoretically omnicompetent, and puts upon the press the burden of accomplishing whatever representative government, industrial organization, and diplomacy have failed to accomplish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques of the press should account for structural limits — readers cannot become informed on every complex issue through episodic news alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend reportable truth by improving institutions and records
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedy... lies in social organization based on a system of analysis and record, and in all the corollaries of that principle; in the abandonment of the theory of the omnicompetent citizen, in the decentralization of decision, in the coordination of decision by comparable record and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improving institutional record-keeping, audits, comparative statistics, and systems of intelligence will enlarge the domain of facts that can be reported precisely and reduce reliance on guesswork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press should signal uncertainty and prod social science and statesmen
rubrics_metrics.description: The task of deflating these controversies, and reducing them to a point where they can be reported as news... It is possible and necessary for journalists to bring home to people the uncertain character of the truth on which their opinions are founded, and by criticism and agitation to prod social science into making more usable formulations of social facts, and to prod statesmen into establishing more visible institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic practice should both report uncertainty candidly and advocate for better institutions and social-scientific work that produce reportable facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of experts in translating impersonal facts for action
rubrics_metrics.description: They break down the drama, break through the stereotypes, and offer men a picture of facts, which is unfamiliar and to them impersonal... They have brought with them... filing cabinets, card catalogues, graphs... and above all the perfectly sound ideal of an executive who sits before a flat-top desk, one sheet of typewritten paper before him, and decides on matters of policy presented in a form ready for his rejection or approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts/statisticians/technicians prepare facts in usable forms (summaries, charts, audits) that make complex institutions intelligible to decision-makers and the press; this work is often dull but necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts must separate knowledge assembly from policy advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The very last thing he will tolerate in his experts is the suspicion that they have a 'policy.' He does not want to know from them whether they like Japanese policy in China. He wants to know what different classes... think about it, and what they are likely to do because of what they think.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expert's authority depends on representing facts and probabilities without partisan advocacy; good diplomatic/intelligence practice divorces assembling of knowledge from decision control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert duty to make the invisible visible (represent intangibles)
rubrics_metrics.description: He represents people who are not voters, functions of voters that are not evident, events that are out of sight, mute people, unborn people, relations between things and people. He has a constituency of intangibles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts should render unseen factors (statistics, correlations, institutional functions) perceptible so that decision-makers and the public can take them into account; by doing so they can materially affect decisions.
